epiphany

ih-PIFF-uh-nee -- four syllables, stress on the second syllable, PIFF. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Epiphany is a moment of sudden insight.

Her epiphany came on the bus: the two data sets had been recorded in different units all along.

Example

For a week the puzzle piece will not fit anywhere. Then, reaching for the salt at dinner, he has his epiphany -- the picture has been upside down on the box the whole time -- and he is out of his chair before the plate stops rattling.

An epiphany is a moment of sudden insight, arriving all at once and usually while you are thinking about something else entirely. It is not slow progress; it is the click.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

breakthrough: A breakthrough is a sudden advance that finally cracks a hard problem -- the wall gives way after long effort, often for a whole team or field. An epiphany happens inside one person: the private flash in which you suddenly understand. Labs announce breakthroughs; you have an epiphany all by yourself.

realization: A realization is the everyday word for coming to know something, and it can arrive at any speed -- including slowly, as a fact gradually dawns on you. An epiphany is a realization at full voltage: it strikes in one dramatic instant and usually changes how you see everything around it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bewilderment: complete confusion

obliviousness: total unawareness

Where it sits · how suddenly the understanding arrives

insight → epiphany → revelation

insight vs. epiphany: Insight can be slow and quiet -- you may build it across a whole semester -- while an epiphany is the single instant in which the understanding lands.

revelation vs. epiphany: A revelation goes beyond an epiphany in the sheer force of its arrival: an epiphany is your own mind clicking into place, but a revelation crashes in from outside -- a hidden letter, a confession -- and rewrites everything at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — epi-: upon, on (Greek)

root — phan-: to show, to appear (Greek phainein)

suffix — -y: state or condition of (Greek -eia)

Put it together: Epiphany comes from Greek epiphaneia, 'appearing, manifestation' -- epi- ('upon') plus phainein ('to show'). An epiphany is an understanding that suddenly shows itself upon you, as though it had walked into the room on its own.

Use the root in a new word: phantom: A phantom of mist drifted across the road and vanished.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Epiphany names the moment, not the idea: you have an epiphany, and what you learn in it is the insight. It suits sudden personal understanding -- about a story, a friendship, a problem you had given up on. Capitalized, Epiphany is also a Christian feast day, but the everyday sense is the lightning-flash one.
